title: An Evening Nap Pushes Your Bedtime Back 80 Mins | Terra
summary: We analyzed 340,889 nights that followed a nap. Before 11 AM a nap costs nothing, but after 5pm it moves bedtime by 80 minutes.
body_markdown:
## Frequent nappers are irregular sleepers


Although 88% of the variation in nap rate is within-people rather than between them, the strongest trait that separates frequent nappers from the rest is how irregularly they sleep.


The standard deviation of bedtime correlates with the probability of tagging a nap at r = +0.336, and an extra hour of bedtime variability comes with 3.5 percentage points more nap-nights. This variability holds on their non-nap days as well, which suggests the variability is not a consequence of napping.


Age is known to alter sleep quality and timing \[3\]. Older users are attributed to lower sleep efficiency, shorter and lighter nights and greater probability of napping. However, bedtime irregularity does not correlate to age which demonstrates this is a trait of common nappers and not a confound of age.


***Figure 2:** (Left) Bedtime variability against how often users nap. (Right) How much each sleep marker moves per decade of age, in standard deviations of that marker.*


This matters beyond napping, because irregular sleep timing is one of the better-evidenced risk markers in sleep research. Cribb et al. (2023) \[2\] followed 88,975 UK Biobank participants for a median of 7.1 years and found that people at the 5th percentile of sleep regularity had a 1.53× higher all-cause mortality hazard than the median, and 1.88× for cardiovascular mortality.


## What actually makes you nap


A day of intense exercise is not the lead cause of napping. If not exercise, then what?


Illness logging dominates and raises the chance of a nap that day by 9.5 percentage points, followed by a cold by 5.9. Tagging behaviors can be a confound themselves, as people tagging illness are more likely to also tag other behaviors like napping.


However, the temperature signal alone is free from this bias, and a hot night with a temperature signal over 1SD from baseline also raises the likelihood of tagging a nap.


***Figure 3:** Change in nap probability with co-occuring events.*


## Conclusion


A long nap does not wreck your night. It moves it. Nap in the morning and you pay nothing; nap after 5pm and you are going to bed an hour and a half later and getting only half of that back by waking later. On top of that, and independently of how long the night ends up being, you spend a couple of minutes less in deep sleep.


And if you want to know why someone napped, the answer is usually that they are ill, that they slept badly, or that they are away from home. It is almost never that they trained hard.
